newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus expels U.S. envoy in new blow to poor ties.
newsitem.headline: Belarus expels U.S. envoy in new blow to poor ties.

text.p: The former Soviet republic of Belarus has expelled a U.S. diplomat who was arrested during clashes between riot police and a crowd of anti-government demonstrators.

A Foreign Ministry statement read of state television on Sunday night said the embassy's first secretary Serzh Alexandrov had committed "provocative actions" during nationalist protests against the pro-Moscow policies of hardline President Alexander Lukashenko.
Washington said that Alexandrov, an ethnic Belarussian, would comply with the expulsion order.
"The Belarus authorities have requested him to depart within 24 hours, and we of course will comply with that wish," a White House official said.

The Foreign Ministry said Alexandrov had been released as soon as his diplomatic identity had been established. About 70 other people were arrested, including two prominent liberal politicians who were also released.
State television said foreign intelligence organs had been involved in the nationalists' rally and said Alexandrov had been working as a spy for the U.S. Central Intelligence Agency.
He added that the U.S. embassy, in violation of all diplomatic norms, had been putting "crude pressure" on the country's Interior Ministry in recent days but gave no further details.
Embassy spokeswoman Janet Demery said Western diplomats often watched Belarus protests from the sidelines "as part of a brief to observe the political situation but not to participate."

The United States has become a vociferous critic of Lukashenko's increasingly authoritarian rule and recently announced it was cutting off $40 million in aid to the country of 10 million because of its human rights performance.
Last week the U.S. embassy protested to Belarus after the local executive director of the Soros Foundation was barred from the country.
State television said that U.S. citizen Peter Bern was accused of supporting the opposition and was barred from re-entering the country for interfering in Belarussian affairs.

The foundation, set up by Hungarian-born American billionaire George Soros, has invested $13 million in Belarus, including $6 million last year mostly for education, ecological and medical programmes.

Sunday's rally was the latest in a series against Lukashenko, a 42-year-old former farm boss who won sweeping powers to shut the old parliament and rewrite the country's constitution last November in a referendum criticised by the West as undemocratic and harmful to human rights.

Popular among many ordinary people who saw their living standards plunge after the collapse of communism, Lukashenko is opposed mainly by a loose union of liberal politicians, nationalists, intellectuals and students mostly in the capital.
He has cracked down on opposition forces by restricting rallies, arresting protesters and putting a senior opposition leader in prison in recent weeks.
The nationalists also object strongly to Lukashenko's building closer ties with Moscow, though most people in the small, land-locked republic support this policy.
The protesters hurled chunks of ice, smashed police car windows and yelled "Long live Belarus!". Police used truncheons and teargas to quell the protests.
